storm.summary_layperson: No storms are on radar anywhere near the cove, the atmosphere has essentially no instability to work with (CAPE pinned at 0), and there are no NWS watches or warnings in effect — a quiet, dry evening for Greenwich and the surrounding towns alike.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer tonight — the Sound (73°F) is already running about 5°F warmer than the air (68°F), the inverse of the setup a sea breeze needs, and the trend model shows that gap only widening (to roughly -10°F) by 7 PM — moot anyway since nothing is approaching to blunt.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar is clear across the region — no echoes at any range and no storm cells tracking toward the cove — and there are no active NWS watches, warnings, or advisories. HRRR has CAPE pinned at 0 J/kg for the whole forecast run, and the OKX area forecast discussion only mentions a slight instability chance (~200 J/kg) well north and west of NYC on Thursday, two days out and not relevant tonight.

The cove's usual defense against storms that do arrive — a stable marine layer that forms when cool Sound water sits under warmer air — isn't available this evening, and the setup is actually inverted: the Sound (73°F) is running about 5°F warmer than the air (68°F) at fetch time. The trend model shows that gap widening further, to roughly -10°F by 7 PM, as air temperatures keep falling after sunset while the water holds steady. A protective layer needs the air to be the warmer side by about 5°F or more; that's nowhere close to being met tonight.

None of this matters much in practice, since there's nothing inbound to blunt or amplify in the first place. Greenwich and the surrounding towns are in the same quiet, dry, high-pressure pattern (1027–1028 hPa) for the whole window.

What would change the call: a new HRRR cycle showing CAPE building overnight, a radar echo appearing to the west or northwest, or an NWS watch/advisory being issued. None of those are currently in play.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient wind, no sea breeze in play — the air-water gap is actually negative (air about 5°F cooler than the Sound, the opposite of what a thermal needs) — so the cove is working with a weak, wandering ENE/E flow in the 3–6 kt range that gets lighter and less certain through the evening. wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a light gradient-wind evening with no sea breeze in play (internal code B-light) — not a thermal day. The two-ingredient sea-breeze test needs both a 5°F+ air-water gap and a favorable gradient; here the gap is actually negative (air 68.0°F vs Sound 73.2°F, a -5.2°F differential), the opposite of what a sea breeze needs, and only 35% of coastal stations show any southerly onshore component. There's no thermal circulation trying to build tonight.

The gradient proxy (mean authoritative station speed) is 5.6 kt, squarely in the light bucket. RYC currently reads SE 136° at 7.4 kt gusting 7.2 (10-min avg just 3.4 kt) — confirming the actual wind at the cove is light and not gusty. Direction agreement across the station ensemble is weak (0.54), and raw HRRR is forecasting a big swing away from the current SE reading toward N/E over the next few hours — a 148° model/obs gap. Since this isn't a sea-breeze day, the maturation correction doesn't apply; we're trusting the observed trend for the next hour or two and leaning on HRRR's ENE/E progression as the best available guide further out, with real uncertainty flagged.

With light ENE-ish flow expected, there's no strong shore preference per the cove geography table — call it a center-of-cove day rather than favoring either bank; the wind is too light for terrain shelter effects to matter much either way.

Speed trends in the 3–6 kt range across the window: 3 kt at 5 PM building slightly to 6 kt near sunset (7:03 PM), the last hour with fresh model data. HRRR's next cycle (f05–f12) failed to fetch, so the 8–10 PM rows are a persistence estimate off the established trend, not fresh model output — confidence is lower for the back half of the window, and light-gradient days like this often go fully variable as the boundary layer stabilizes after dark. Fleet impact: 3–6 kt is drifter territory for one-designs, finicky but technically raceable early; by 9–10 PM it's marginal, postponement-risk territory if it drops toward 2–3 kt or goes fully variable.
